nodes.name: Periodic function
nodes.statement: A function f is periodic with period T when f(t + T) = f(t) for every t.

nodes.name: Sinusoid
nodes.statement: A sinusoid A sin(2πft + φ) is fixed by three numbers: its amplitude A, its frequency f and its phase φ.

nodes.name: Harmonics
nodes.statement: The waves cos(nωt) and sin(nωt), with ω = 2π/T and n a whole number, all repeat with period T. Any sum of them is also T-periodic.

nodes.name: Functions as vectors
nodes.statement: Functions on an interval can be treated as vectors. The integral ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫ f(t)g(t) dt plays the role of the dot product.

nodes.name: Orthogonality
nodes.statement: Over one period, the integral of the product of two different harmonics is zero. The harmonics behave like perpendicular axes.

nodes.name: Harmonics as a basis
nodes.statement: Writing a function as a sum of harmonics is like writing a vector as a sum of components along perpendicular axes.

nodes.name: Fourier series
nodes.statement: A well-behaved periodic function can be written as f(t) = a₀/2 + Σ (aₙ cos(nωt) + bₙ sin(nωt)), summed over n = 1, 2, 3 and so on.

nodes.name: Coefficient formula
nodes.statement: Each coefficient is the projection of f onto its harmonic. For example aₙ = (2/T) ∫ f(t) cos(nωt) dt over one period, and bₙ uses sin in the same way.

nodes.name: Euler's formula
nodes.statement: Euler's formula says e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ, so e^(iωt) traces a circle at steady speed.

nodes.name: Complex exponential form
nodes.statement: With Euler's formula the series becomes f(t) = Σ cₙ e^(inωt), where n runs over all integers, negative ones included.

nodes.name: Spinning circles picture
nodes.statement: Each term cₙ e^(inωt) is an arrow spinning n times per period. Adding all the arrows tip to tail traces out f(t).

nodes.name: Even and odd symmetry
nodes.statement: An even function has only cosine terms and an odd function has only sine terms, because the other integrals cancel over a symmetric period.

nodes.name: Square wave series
nodes.statement: A square wave switching between −1 and +1 equals (4/π)(sin ωt + (1/3) sin 3ωt + (1/5) sin 5ωt + ...). It contains only odd harmonics.

nodes.name: Smoothness and decay
nodes.statement: The smoother a function is, the faster its coefficients shrink as n grows. A jump gives coefficients falling like 1/n, and a kink gives 1/n².

nodes.name: Sharp edges need high frequencies
nodes.statement: Sharp corners and jumps can only be reproduced with many high-frequency harmonics.

nodes.name: Pointwise convergence
nodes.statement: For a piecewise smooth function, the Fourier series converges to f(t) wherever f is continuous. At a jump it converges to the midpoint of the jump.

nodes.name: Gibbs phenomenon
nodes.statement: Near a jump, a truncated Fourier series overshoots by about 9% of the jump size. Adding more terms makes the overshoot narrower but not smaller.

nodes.name: Parseval's theorem
nodes.statement: The average of |f(t)|² over one period equals Σ |cₙ|². The signal's energy is split exactly among its frequencies.

nodes.name: Best approximation
nodes.statement: Keeping the terms up to harmonic N gives the smallest possible mean squared error among all sums of those harmonics.

nodes.name: Derivatives multiply by inω
nodes.statement: Differentiating f multiplies each coefficient cₙ by inω, so differentiation becomes simple multiplication on the coefficients.

nodes.name: Fourier's heat problem
nodes.statement: Fourier created the series to solve the heat equation. In a ring or rod, each harmonic decays on its own at a rate proportional to n².

nodes.name: Heat smooths fast wiggles
nodes.statement: Under heat flow the high harmonics fade fastest, so a temperature profile becomes smoother over time.

nodes.name: Sinusoids survive linear systems
nodes.statement: A linear time-invariant system turns a sinusoid into a sinusoid of the same frequency, changing only its amplitude and phase.

nodes.name: Filtering
nodes.statement: A linear filter can be analysed one harmonic at a time. Each output coefficient is the input coefficient times the filter's response at that frequency.

nodes.name: Spectrum
nodes.statement: The coefficient sizes |cₙ| plotted against frequency nω form the signal's spectrum, which shows how much of each frequency it contains.

nodes.name: Timbre
nodes.statement: A violin and a flute playing the same note share the same fundamental frequency. They sound different because their harmonics have different strengths.

nodes.name: Fourier transform
nodes.statement: Letting the period T grow without bound packs the harmonics into a continuous spectrum. The result is the Fourier transform, which handles signals that never repeat.
